name: Chestmaxxing / chest-out posture

lead: Chest-out posture is an open, upright stance with the chest raised and shoulders back. In looksmaxxing it is used to make the upper body look broader and more confident right away while held.

The chain is the chest held open and raised, shoulders back so the torso looks fuller, then a confident, broader upper body. Psychology references describe open posture as generally perceived as friendly and positive, and in one self-validation study participants in a confident posture rated their own qualities more favourably. No trial has tested chest-out posture as a way to change perceived attractiveness.

paras: People practise holding the chest and shoulders in an expanded position while standing and sitting, often alongside back and shoulder strength work, until it becomes a habit. The term is also used for building chest size, which is a separate training topic.

No specific harms are documented in the sources found. Holding a forced, exaggerated position for long periods can feel tiring, and underlying medical conditions are worth ruling out if posture is hard to hold.

angle.text: Chestmaxxing means standing with the chest open and raised and shoulders back, which visibly makes the upper body look broader and more confident while held. Open posture is generally read as confident; the term itself has little formal study.

lead: Chestmaxxing or chest-out posture refers to carrying the chest open and raised as part of a posture-focused approach to appearance. Sources specific to the term are very limited.

A general psychology reference states that open posture, with a raised head and spread limbs, is often perceived as communicating a friendly and positive attitude, while closed posture is associated with an impression of detachment or disinterest.[1] In one self-validation study cited there, participants in a confident posture rated their own qualities more favourably than those in a doubtful posture.[1]
No published trial has tested chest-out posture as a way to change perceived attractiveness.

paras: Open posture is described as often perceived as communicating a friendly and positive attitude, and counsellors using it were seen as more capable of giving guidance.[1] The same reference cautions that posture should be read together with other cues and cultural norms, and that medical conditions should be ruled out before drawing conclusions about personality.[1]
